text: The Line of Control (LoC) is a de facto military boundary between Indian- and Pakistani-controlled regions of the former princely state of Jammu and Kashmir, established as part of the Simla Agreement following the Indo-Pakistani War of 1971. Though not a legally recognized international boundary, it replaced the original 1949 ceasefire line with a renamed "Line of Control" that both nations agreed to respect without prejudice to their positions. The Indian-controlled areas are divided into the union territories of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, while the Pakistani-controlled areas are Azad Kashmir and Gilgit–Baltistan. The northernmost point of the LoC is NJ9842, beyond which lies the Siachen Glacier, a site of armed clashes beginning in 1984. To the south, the border between Pakistani Punjab and the Jammu province is ambiguous: India considers it an "international boundary," while Pakistan refers to it as a "working border." A separate ceasefire line, known as the Line of Actual Control (LAC), separates Indian-controlled Jammu and Kashmir from Chinese-controlled Aksai Chin. After the 1947 First Kashmir War and the 1965 conflict, only minor changes were made to the original ceasefire line, with the 1972 Simla Agreement formalizing the LoC as a de facto border and stipulating that neither side would unilaterally alter it, regardless of differences in legal interpretation. The United Nations Military Observer Group in India and Pakistan (UNMOGIP) was tasked with investigating ceasefire violations (CFVs), though its role diminished after 1971. In 2000, U.S. President Bill Clinton identified the Kashmir Line of Control as one of the world’s most dangerous regions. The LoC from Kargil to Gurez includes mountain passes and valleys with streams and rivers; areas up to 14,000 feet (4,300 m) are wooded, while higher peaks are exposed, with snowy winters and mild summers. From Gurez to Akhnoor, the terrain is mountainous and hilly, generally forested, with tracks and minor roads connecting settlements. Visibility and line of sight are significantly affected by the mix of flora and elevation. In 2018, two corps and multiple battalions of the Border Security Force manned the Indian side, while the Rawalpindi Corps guarded the Pakistani side. CFVs occur symmetrically on both sides, and responses to one incident can trigger firing at distant locations. Weapons used include small arms, rocket-propelled grenades, recoilless rifles, mortars, automatic grenade launchers, rocket launchers, and other direct and indirect arms. Soldiers face sniper attacks in moving vehicles, through bunker peepholes, and during meals. Civilian populations living near or ahead of forward posts have complicated the situation, with shelling and firing resulting in civilian deaths. Bunkers have been built for civilian protection during CFVs. India and Pakistan typically report only their own side’s casualties, blaming the other for firing and claiming adequate retaliation. According to Happymon Jacob, CFVs stem from operational reasons (such as defense construction, the "rule of the gun," lack of bilateral border mechanisms, and soldier or commander traits), politico-strategic motives, proportional responses (like land grabs, revenge firing, or "I am better than you"), accidental incidents (civilian-related or unclear line demarcation), and other factors (testing new recruits, honor, prestige, humiliation, fun, gamesmanship), with operational reasons being the primary cause. Mines were laid across the India–Pakistan border and the LoC in 1947, 1965, 1971, and 2001; the small stretch between fencing rows is mined with thousands of landmines. During the 2001–2002 standoff, thousands of acres along the LoC were mined, leading to civilian and military deaths and injuries. Between January 2000 and April 2002, 138 Indian military personnel were killed. Reinforced sandbagged and concrete posts and bunkers serve as the first line of defense, equipped with supplies for at least a week, allowing soldiers to sleep, cook, and monitor enemy positions continuously. Some posts are in remote locations, with animals used for transport or reared on-site. Living quarters and forward bunkers are often separated, and some post locations follow old 1947–1972 war-era positions with minor adjustments. India constructed a 550-kilometre (340 mi) Anti-Infiltration Obstacle System (AIOS) barrier along a 740–776 km stretch of the LoC by 2004, consisting of double rows of fencing, concertina wire 8–12 feet (2.4–3.7 m) high, electrified, and linked to motion sensors, thermal imaging, lighting, and alarms. Construction began in the 1990s, slowed in the early 2000s due to increased hostilities, resumed after a November 2003 ceasefire, and was completed in late 2004. The fence reduced militant infiltration by 80%, according to Indian military sources, and a proposal for an upgraded smart fence was accepted in 2017. Pakistan has not built a border fence, though several villages lie between the Indian fence and the zero line—13 in Tithwal, with an estimated total of 60 villages and at least one million people living in districts adjacent to the LoC from Rajouri to Bandipora. The Indian Ministry of Home Affairs reported 1,504 "terrorist" infiltration attempts in 2002, with only 105 successful ones in 2016. Infiltration was a key issue during the 2001–2002 standoff, and the reduction in such attempts reflects declining support within Pakistan. During the 2019 Balakot airstrike, Indian aircraft crossed the LoC for the first time in 48 years. Following the 2005 Kashmir earthquake, five official crossing points were designated: Nauseri-Tithwal, Chakoti-Uri, Hajipur-Uri, Rawalakot-Poonch, and Tattapani-Mendhar. The 2016 Azad Jammu and Kashmir Cross LoC Travel and Trade Authority Act lists trade points including Chakothi–Salamabad and Rawalakot (Titrinote)–Poonch (Chakkan-da-Bagh), with the 2011 ordinance establishing these. Between 2005 and 2017, approximately 14,000 people crossed from Muzaffarabad to Indian Kashmir, while about 22,000 crossed to Pakistan. Legal crossings require extensive documentation, including proof of family ties, and even temporary crossings invite government scrutiny. Security forces hold flag meetings and exchange sweets during festivals at these points. On 21 October 2008, cross-LoC trade was conducted for the first time in 61 years. Trade is barter-based, with nearly PKR 11,446 crore (₹5,000 crore or US$790 million in 2023) passing through Chakothi–Salamabad in ten years. The Teetwal crossing, across the Neelum River between Muzaffarabad and Kupwara, is open only in summer and for people, not trade. The Tithwal bridge, first built in 1931, has been rebuilt twice. The Salamabad crossing (Kamran Post) is a major trade and travel route in the Baramulla district, with banking and trade facilitation centers planned on the Indian side. The bridge, named "bridge of peace" in English, was rebuilt after the 2005 earthquake when a mountain collapsed on the Pakistani side and reopened for trade in 2008. The Srinagar–Muzaffarabad bus crosses this bridge. A road connects Kotli and Tatrinote on the Pakistani side to the Indian Poonch district via Chakan Da Bagh, a major trade and travel route with planned banking and trade centers. Most flag meetings occur here. The Tattapani–Mendhar crossing was opened on 14 November 2005. The LoC division severed the Jhelum valley route, the only access from Pakistani Punjab to the Kashmir Valley, cutting off villages and separating families. Some families could see each other across the LoC, such as along the Neelum River, but could not meet. Women on the Pakistani side have sometimes approached military camps to demand an end to infiltration, reducing Indian cross-LoC firing. Documentaries covering the LoC include *A journey through River Vitasta*, *Raja Shabir Khan's Line of Control*, and *HistoryTV18's Kargil: Valour & Victory*. Bollywood films depicting the LoC include *LOC: Kargil* (2003), *Lakshya* (2004), *Gunjan Saxena: The Kargil Girl* (2020), *Uri: The Surgical Strike* (2019), and *Bajrangi Bhaijaan* (2015), as well as the TV show *Avrodh* (2020). The coordinates of the LoC are 34°56′N 76°46′E / 34.933°N 76.767°E / 34.933; 76.767.
